verdicts.reason: Alternative considered: the 'generic fixed-capacity pooled-entity constructor' at arm9:0x020834D4 could actually be a sound-effect pool, UI-widget pool, or other non-battle allocator that merely happens to be reused from ov6, rather than a battle-hitbox/projectile pool. Tested by tracing callers and the actual field writes made through the returned entity: xrefs-to 0x0214BE14 (the manager global) show all 31 references confined to a single tight arm9 module 0x02083434-0x02083C98, reached only via the trampoline 0x02083624 (22 callers: 20 in ov6 spanning 0x02156Bxx-0x02170Cxx, plus arm9:0x02085704 the hitbox-processing loop itself) and 3 direct callers of 0x020834D4 (0x02164F0C/0x02164F48/0x02168E44, all ov6). Disassembling the actual call sites at 0x02164EA0-0x02165044 (immediately around 0x02164F0C/0x02164F48) shows the newly-acquired entity's +0x30 field (the constructor-callback return value) is a record that gets a hit-tally-style halfword written (+0x20 = 0x12c/0x4b), category-exclusive bit flags passed as r3 (#0x8000 vs #0x4000, disjoint single-bit hitbox-type tags), a vtable dereference and blx call ([r8+4]->+0x68->[0]->+0x6c), and a decrementing counter at [sb+0x100+0x4e] gated to 4 states -- this is battle hit/effect bookkeeping, not audio or UI. No caller context anywhere touches sound-channel or UI-widget structures. Alternative loses; claim's own hedged 'generic pooled-entity' framing (shared by other spawned hitbox/effect objects, not exclusively projectiles) is exactly what the evidence supports.

Alternative considered: the +0x10 field / callee pair (0x0207c988 in the constructor, 0x0207cb58 in the destructor at 0x02083648) could be a generic, widely-shared hook mechanism reused by unrelated subsystems, which would weaken the claim's tight alloc/free symmetry framing; also considered that 0x0207cb58 is literally called through +0x10 as claimed. Tested via callers: 0x0207c988 has exactly 1 static caller (0x020834D4, the constructor) and 0x0207cb58 has exactly 1 static caller (0x02083648, the destructor) -- an exclusive 1:1 acquire/release pairing private to this alloc/free pair, ruling out cross-subsystem hook reuse. However, re-disassembling 0x02083648 directly shows the real mechanics are 'ldr r0,[r4,#0x10]; bl 0x207cb58' -- a direct (non-indirect) call to a fixed function that takes [entity+0x10] as its argument, not an indirect call THROUGH +0x10 as the claim's prose states ('calls an on-destroy hook via the entity's +0x10 field'); 0x0207cb58's body (a 3-slot table walk with bl 0x2037c24/0x2037b98 list operations) looks like release of a paired sub-resource acquired by 0x0207c988, not a virtual/indirect callback. This is a minor mischaracterization of the calling convention, not a misidentification of the function's role -- the destroy-primitive identity, the +0xc/+0x1c list unlink/append symmetry with the constructor's failure path, and the 32-caller footprint (2 arm9 + 30 ov6, matching the claim's count exactly, including all four Q3 kill sites) all hold up, so the alternative (unrelated generic hook) is refuted and the core claim stands despite the prose imprecision.

Alternative considered: the 13-way switch at ov6:0x021574CC could be a generic animation-state or frame-event dispatcher invoked for every character action (idle/walk/block/etc.), not specifically an attack/projectile-spawn dispatcher -- which would undercut reading case index 8 as 'an attack fires'. Tested via xrefs-to 0x021574CC (exactly 1 literal_load, at ov6:0x02156AFC) and its context: the dispatcher's address is stored into [r1+0x5e8] of an object loaded from [r5] inside a per-move initialization routine (r5 is that routine's own argument, and r4 -- the character struct -- is stored into the adjacent +0x5ec field of the same object), i.e. it is registered as a per-MOVE event-handler slot, not a per-character/per-frame generic callback. Further, disassembling case index 8's body (0x02157684-0x02157838) shows it is gated by a check at 0x0215765C-0x02157678 that reads character+0x1ac and bails out if already non-zero (a 'one active spawn at a time' cap), then after the entity-pool call at 0x02157700 (bl 0x2168cf4, confirmed as the Q1 constructor's caller) stores the new wrapper pointer back into character+0x1ac at 0x021577E0 -- a concrete spawn-with-cap-of-one pattern that fits a projectile/summon slot, not a generic animation tick. The animation-dispatcher alternative loses; the claim's dispatcher-mechanics description (jump table, per-move collision-entry bytes at [r8+0x1a]/[r8+0x1b] feeding the call, no intervening conditional branch to the bl at 0x02157700) is confirmed instruction-for-instruction against the re-disassembled listing.

Alternative considered: the value written to wrapper+0xc at ov6:0x02168E5C (claimed to be an 'ownership back-pointer' to the attacking character's MoveInfo object) could instead be a small scalar like a team index or palette-slot byte, which would refute the ownership-pointer reading. Tested by disassembling the full body of 0x02168CF4: the same register (r4, the function's 2nd argument, identical to the value stored at +0xc) is dereferenced repeatedly as a structured pointer before the store -- at entry 'ldr r1,[r4,#0x10]; ldr r6,[r1,#0x5c]' obtains a collision/position sub-object, and r6's +0xc/+0x10 fields are read and combined with per-frame deltas via bl 0x20836B4 (collision-box overlap test) twice more before the wrapper is even allocated. A team-index or palette-slot value (0-3ish) dereferenced at offset +0x10 would almost certainly fault or read garbage; instead every use is consistent with a valid heap/struct pointer, matching the claim's identification of r4 as the character's MoveInfo pointer (loaded from character+0x1a8 by the caller immediately before the call, per claim 2's own evidence at ov6:0x021576FC). Alternative refuted. Bonus finding (not required for this verdict but relevant to the claim's own open question about a more direct character back-pointer): the dispatcher caller at 0x02157720 additionally stores r4 -- the raw CHARACTER struct pointer, not MoveInfo -- into wrapper+0x18 right after the wrapper returns from 0x2168cf4, so a direct character-struct back-pointer does exist, just on the wrapper (+0x18) rather than inside the pooled entity itself, and is written by the caller rather than by 0x02168CF4.

Alternative considered: ov6:0x0216C958 could be the per-frame update/despawn routine for a DIFFERENT spawned-effect kind (e.g. a hit-spark or dust-particle entity that shares the same generic pool infrastructure), not specifically the projectile entity traced in the Q1/Q2/Q4 claims -- exactly the open question the claim itself flags as unresolved. Tested via callers/callees: the movement-delta accessor 0x216B740 (which supplies r4 in this function) has 20 call sites across roughly 10 sibling functions clustered at 0x0216B5xx-0x0216CFxx, and the boundary-test helper 0x216EE14 (used in kill-condition (a)) is independently called from 3 different functions (0x0216C958, 0x0216E1C0, 0x0216F398) -- i.e. this exact per-frame-check scaffolding (movement update + generic destroy-condition checks) is reused near-identically by multiple distinct spawned-object update routines in ov6, and no static evidence (no caller edge from the Q2/Q4 spawn path, no shared literal/constant) links 0x0216C958 specifically to the projectile-class entity rather than one of its siblings. Additionally, re-disassembling condition (c)/(d) shows both thresholds (0x100 and 0x0003FF00, loaded at 0x0216CAC0) gate the SAME field r4[0] as a two-sided [low,high] bounds check, and r4 itself is populated by adding per-frame deltas (from an r5 array, i.e. velocity-like values) into r4[0]/r4[4] at 0x0216C9D0-0x0216C9E8 before being written into what looks like a position record ([[entity+0x10]+0x5c]+0xc/+0x10) -- this reads more like a position/world-bounds despawn check than the claim's hedged 'hit counter' candidate, refining but not resolving the open question. Cannot discriminate statically which sibling function is 'the' projectile despawn routine, so this is UNSURE rather than UPHELD or REFUTED; the mechanical description of the four kill sites converging on arm9:0x02083648 is itself accurate and independently corroborated (all four call addresses appear verbatim in 0x02083648's 32-caller list from claim 1).
